content:
Hi all — I opened physlib#1441: a proposal to make Physlib.Units.Dimension parametric in its set of base dimensions. I'd welcome feedback on the design — I think the need is fairly clear-cut, so the real question is how best to do it.

Today a dimension is a fixed record of five ℚ exponents over a hardwired basis — length, time, mass, charge, temperature. The exponent type is already ℚ (nice — half-integer powers work), but the basis — its rank and the identity of its generators — is baked in, and that turns out to be a genuine limitation, not a cosmetic one:

  • It isn't even the SI/ISQ basis: it takes charge rather than electric current, and has no amount-of-substance or luminous-intensity axis — so PhysLib can't faithfully represent the ISQ's own seven base quantities.
  • Systems with a different generating set are simply inexpressible: Gaussian–CGS (three generators, charge derived as M^(1/2)·L^(3/2)·T^(-1)), natural units, and so on.
  • And there is a sustained, serious case in the metrology literature — roughly a decade of Metrologia papers (Quincey–Mohr–Phillips, Leonard, Kalinin, Mills, …) — for giving angle its own base dimension, with solid angle as its square (sr = rad²), to eliminate spurious factors of 2π. That reform can't even be expressed over a fixed basis.

So the current basis quietly commits to one contested metrological stance and rules out others that are entirely standard — which is what makes a parametric basis feel necessary rather than optional.

The encouraging part is that it looks cheap and contained. The Dimension type lives almost entirely within Physlib/Units/ (~12 files), and a quick prototype suggests the algebra comes essentially for free from Mathlib:

abbrev Dimension (B : Type) := Multiplicative (B → ℚ)
example {B : Type} : CommGroup (Dimension B) := inferInstance   -- from Pi, no boilerplate

The present basis is recovered as Dimension PhyslibBase over a concrete enum; backward compatibility can go through a thin wrapper keeping the named projections and @[simp] lemmas, so existing Units/ code compiles unchanged.

Where I'd genuinely value input is the shape of the fix:

  • Is Multiplicative (B → ℚ) (or B →₀ ℚ) the right core, or is there a cleaner representation?
  • Replace Dimension, or add the parametric type alongside behind a deprecation window?
  • One library-wide basis vs. per-development? (HasDim M currently implies a single shared basis.)
  • How should the parallel UnitChoices / dimScale — which hardwire the same five bases — follow?

The issue has the full write-up, a requirements checklist, the corresponding-file map, and a compile-checked prototype. Does the parametric-B direction look right, or would you shape it differently?

There was some talk a while ago about how to define dimensions and nothing was really decided, what currently exists is more of a test than anything and that is why it isn't used anywhere else. I think we'd agree that having the ability use a more dynamic unit system would be better. The problem is no one has a good proposal for how to link dimensions to a scalar value. E.g. if I have a position function $x(t)$, how do we encore the information that the input has dimension time and the output has dimension length? What exists now is proof of concept of one way to do so and is definitely incomplete in many ways. If you have an idea how to do that with your proposal we'd be happy to see it

The problem is no one has a good proposal for how to link dimensions to a scalar value. E.g. if I have a position function $x(t)$, how do we encode the information that the input has dimension time and the output has dimension length?

Daniel Morrison — agreed that the hard part is linking a value to its dimension (your x(t): dimension time in, dimension length out), not the choice of basis. I'd tease it into two axes, because I think they're independent:

  • What the basis of Dimension is — the rank and identity of the group's generators. That's all this issue touches.
  • How a value is linked to its dimension — your x(t). That's a wrapper over Dimension, not a change to it.

You can change the basis without touching the value-linking machinery, and change the value-linking without touching the basis — so I don't think the (harder, very real) value-linking question blocks the basis change, which is cheap and contained. The two axes only touch in one place — see the end.

On the linking problem itself, the design space I've found useful splits two ways:

1. Index the value by its dimension. Quantity (d : Dimension) (α : Type), with mul : Quantity d₁ α → Quantity d₂ α → Quantity (d₁ * d₂) α. Then x : Quantity 𝖳 ℝ → Quantity 𝖫 ℝ and the dimensional constraint just rides the function arrow — the type system carries it, no extra machinery. The whole ergonomic cost sits in the index: d₁ * d₂ is a computed group element, so unless Dimension has canonical normal forms with good DecidableEq/defeq, every product spawns a coercion or a proof obligation. This is the one spot the
two axes meet: a Multiplicative (B → ℚ) / B →₀ ℚ representation (what the issue proposes) hands you those normal forms essentially for free from Mathlib's Pi/Finsupp instances — which is what makes a dimension-indexed value type tractable rather than painful. So a clean parametric Dimension is a prerequisite for your question, not a competitor to it.

2. Index by something finer than the dimension, with a homomorphism to Dimension. The motivation is that dimension is lossy: physically distinct quantities collapse to the same element (torque vs. energy; and every dimension-one quantity — plane angle, solid angle, a bare ratio — is the same element, which is a big part of why the angle-reform literature is unhappy). If a value is indexed directly by Dimension, the type system can't separate those. So you index by a finer classifier k, provide dim : k → Dimension as a proven
homomorphism, and keep the numeric carrier as an orthogonal parameter, Quantity k (R : Type). x(t) is still an ordinary typed function Q A R → Q B R, but now the same value can be held at R = ℝ for proofs and
R = Float for execution without touching the dimensional index.

Both make x(t) a plain typed function; the choice is really how much you want the index to distinguish. But either way the value layer wants a Dimension with canonical normal forms underneath it — so I read your point as more reason to get the representation right, not a reason to defer it.

I think your proposal is fine if you want to try to implement it, I don't think there's a reason that this hasn't been added other than no one has done it yet. I like the use of Multiplicative to show that multiplying dimensions leads to adding the exponents. Defining an inductive type for the dimensions seems like a good idea too. I don't know of a situation where you have an infinite collection of dimensions so I think using Fintype is okay.

One problem we ran into before was that some dimensions were propositionally equal but not definitionally equal: for instance I should be able to compare a quantity with dimension meters with a product of elements with dimension meters/second and second but Lean didn't realize the types were the same. In that sense the implementation of Dimension does impact the definition of Quantity down the road. But again, if you think you have a good idea please implement as much as you can!

Thanks @Daniel Morrison for the encouragement and the constructive discussion!

I implemented my proposal in PR #1447 with an example of the problem you raised: Physlib/Units/ParametricDimensionExamples.lean.
